info.name: FAHLA 2026 WS3 — FHIR Exploration (Rico)
info.description:
Postman collection for FAHLA 2026 Workshop 3: Interoperability — Challenges and Solutions.

Target: HAPI FHIR public test server ([https://cdr.fhirlab.net/fhir](https://cdr.fhirlab.net/fhir)).

Flow:

1. Server CapabilityStatement — what can this server do?
    
2. Search patients by name — the name-collision problem
    
3. Retrieve a Patient resource — what FHIR looks like
    
4. Search observations — filtering by code (LOINC)
    
5. POST Rico's Patient resource — create on a scratch server
    
6. GET Rico back — verify round-trip
    
7. Search by identifier system — the identifier namespace problem (Scenario 1)
    

All requests use the public HAPI test server. Data you POST is visible to everyone and may be wiped at any time. DO NOT post real patient data.

request.description:
Every FHIR server must publish what it can do. This is the 'menu.'

Look for:
- software.name, software.version
- rest[0].resource — every resource type supported
- format — which serializations (json, xml)

Teaching moment: this is the DISCOVERABILITY that HL7 v2 never had.

item.name: 2. Search Patients by name (the collision problem)

request.description:
How many 'Rico Dela Cruz' patients exist on this public server? Probably many.

Teaching moment: name matching is not patient matching. This is exactly the problem a Master Patient Index / PhilSys linkage solves (Scenario 1 in the exercise).

The classic FHIR Patient/example resource. Note the structure:
- resourceType, id, meta
- identifier (system + value — NOT just value)
- name (use, family, given)
- telecom, gender, birthDate, address

Teaching moment: every field has a DEFINED place. Compare to a free-text clinical note.

Search for every body weight observation on the server.

Note the search syntax: code=SYSTEM|CODE. The code alone is ambiguous. The system+code pair is globally unique.

Teaching moment: this is semantic interoperability in action. Any server in the world that implemented the same standard would return the same conceptual answer.

Create Rico on the public test server.

Response headers include 'Location:' — that is your new resource URL. Copy the assigned id for step 6.

Teaching moment: server assigns the id. Your local id 'PH-TB-2026-0142' lives in the identifier field, not in the id. The distinction matters — id is server-scoped; identifier is business-scoped.

Search Rico back using our OWN identifier system — not the server-assigned id.

This is the round trip. In production, this is exactly how one facility would retrieve a patient that another facility created.

Teaching moment: without the identifier 'system' URL, you are searching by a string that could belong to anyone.

Same identifier VALUE. Different identifier SYSTEM. Result: no match.

This is Scenario 1 in your exercise packet. The receiving hospital assumed the identifier belongs to its own namespace. It doesn't.

Teaching moment: semantic standards can't fix this. Syntactic compliance can't fix this. Only identifier governance — a Master Patient Index or a national identity layer (PhilSys) — can. This is why WHO SMART Guideline L3 needs an L4 that includes governance.

Fetch body-weight observations AND the patients they reference, in one call.

The response is a searchset Bundle with entry[].search.mode = 'match' or 'include'.

Teaching moment: FHIR references are lazy. The observation doesn't repeat patient data — it points to it. _include tells the server to materialize the references so your client doesn't make N extra calls.
